claim: Mutations in coding and non-coding regions of FUS cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Mutations in coding and non-coding regions of FUS cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established scientific knowledge about FUS mutations causing ALS.

claim: Mutations in the 3'-UTR of FUS lead to increased FUS accumulation and are causal for ALS.
source: Intriguingly, mutations in the 3'-UTR of FUS leading to elevated FUS accumulation are known to be causal for ALS (Sabatelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sabatelli et al., 2013.

claim: Broad expression of wild-type or ALS-linked mutant human FUS in mice produces progressive motor phenotypes accompanied by ALS-like pathology.
source: We show here that broad expression within the nervous system of wild-type or either of two ALS-linked mutants of human FUS in mice produces progressive motor phenotypes accompanied by characteristic ALS-like pathology.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Human FUS downregulates endogenous mouse FUS at mRNA and protein levels through an autoregulatory mechanism.
source: FUS levels are autoregulated by a mechanism in which human FUS downregulates endogenous FUS at mRNA and protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E, and G.

claim: Increasing wild-type human FUS expression by saturating the autoregulatory mechanism produces a rapidly progressive phenotype and dose-dependent lethality.
source: Increasing wild-type human FUS expression achieved by saturating this autoregulatory mechanism produces a rapidly progressive phenotype and dose-dependent lethality.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Transcriptome analysis reveals mis-regulation of genes that are largely not observed upon FUS reduction.
source: Transcriptome analysis reveals mis-regulation of genes that are largely not observed upon FUS reduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and comparative analysis shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Likely mechanisms for FUS neurotoxicity include autophagy inhibition and defective RNA metabolism.
source: Likely mechanisms for FUS neurotoxicity include autophagy inhibition and defective RNA metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on autophagy (Figure 9) and RNA metabolism (Figure 6).

claim: Overriding FUS autoregulation triggers gain-of-function toxicity via altered autophagy-lysosome pathway and RNA metabolism function.
source: Thus, our results reveal that overriding FUS autoregulation will trigger gain-of-function toxicity via altered autophagy-lysosome pathway and RNA metabolism function, highlighting a role for protein and RNA dyshomeostasis in FUS-mediated toxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: TDP-43 is a major component of ubiquitinated aggregates in ALS and FTLD patients.
source: The landmark discovery of TAR-DNA binding protein (TDP-43) as a major component of ubiquitinated aggregates in ALS and FTLD (frontotemporal lobar degeneration, a term used to stress the pathological classification of FTD) patients (Neumann et al., 2006; Arai et al., 2006) led to the identification of ALS and FTD-causing mutations in the genes encoding two nucleic acid-binding proteins, TDP-43 (Sreedharan et al., 2008; Kabashi et al., 2008; Van Deerlin et al., 2008) and fused in sarcoma/translocated in liposarcoma (FUS/TLS) (hereafter referred to as FUS) (Kwiatkowski et al., 2009; Vance et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neumann et al., 2006 and Arai et al., 2006.

claim: FUS is a 526 amino acid protein containing a prion-like low-complexity domain, nuclear export signal, RNA recognition motif domain, arginine/glycine-rich domains, zinc-finger motif, and nuclear localization signal.
source: Molecularly, FUS is a 526 amino acid protein containing a prion-like low-complexity domain (Kato et al., 2012; Cushman et al., 2010), followed by a nuclear export signal, a RNA recognition motif (RRM) domain, arginine/glycine (R/G)-rich domains, a zinc-finger motif and nuclear localization signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kato et al., 2012 and Cushman et al., 2010, and represents established knowledge about FUS structure.

claim: 48 out of 60 ALS/FTD causing mutations in FUS are clustered in the extreme C-terminus containing the PY-NLS.
source: A preponderance of the ALS/FTD causing mutations (48 out of 60) is clustered in the FUS extreme C-terminus that contains its non-canonical nuclear localization signal (known as PY-NLS) (Dormann et al., 2010; Lattante et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dormann et al., 2010 and Lattante et al., 2013.

claim: FUS mutants result in increased cytosolic accumulation which correlates with disease severity.
source: Correspondingly, such FUS mutants have been shown to result in increased cytosolic accumulation which correlates with disease severity (Dormann et al., 2010; Bosco et al., 2010; Gal et al., 2011; Vance et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions of FUS are found in ALS patients with mutations in FUS.
source: Neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions of FUS are found in ALS patients with mutations in FUS (Kwiatkowski et al., 2009; Vance et al., 2009; Dormann et al., 2010), suggesting that (i) disturbing the nuclear-cytosolic distribution can lead to FUS proteinopathy, and (ii) loss of nuclear RNA processing functions may contribute to ALS pathogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kwiatkowski et al., 2009; Vance et al., 2009; and Dormann et al., 2010.

claim: FUS knockout mice do not develop ALS disease phenotypes.
source: However, Kino and colleagues used outbred FUS knockout mice to show that these FUS knockout mice do not develop ALS disease phenotypes (Kino et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kino et al., 2015.

claim: Mice expressing disease-causing FUS mutations or FUS with NLS-deletions developed motor neuron degeneration.
source: In contrast, mice expressing disease-causing FUS mutations or FUS with NLS-deletions developed motor neuron degeneration, favoring a 'gain-of-toxic properties' model (Scekic-Zahirovic et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016; Shiihashi et al., 2016; Devoy et al., 2017; López-Erauskin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Autophagy dysfunction has been implicated in various neurodegenerative diseases, including ALS.
source: Not surprisingly, autophagy dysfunction has been implicated in various neurodegenerative diseases, including ALS (Wong and Cuervo, 2010; Nixon and Yang, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wong and Cuervo, 2010 and Nixon and Yang, 2012.

claim: Numerous ALS-FTD genes are involved in autophagy regulation, including SQSTM1, OPTN, TBK1, and VCP.
source: The notion that autophagy dysfunction contributes to ALS-FTD pathogenesis is strongly supported by the identification of numerous ALS-FTD genes involved in autophagy regulation, including SQSTM1 (Fecto et al., 2011), OPTN (Maruyama et al., 2010; Wong and Holzbaur, 2014), TBK1 (Cirulli et al., 2015; Freischmidt et al., 2015; Pottier et al., 2015), and VCP (Johnson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Loss of TDP-43 inhibits autophagy by blocking the fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes.
source: Intriguingly, recent work has shown that loss of TDP-43 inhibits autophagy by blocking the fusion of autophagosomes with lysosomes (Xia et al., 2016), and that enhancing autophagy may be beneficial for mice modeling TDP-43 proteinopathies (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xia et al., 2016 and Wang et al., 2012.

claim: Twelve transgenic FUS mouse lines were established from 34 founders.
source: Twelve lines were established from 34 founders (three wild type lines from seven founders, 5 R514G lines from 13 founders, and 4 R521C lines from 14 founders).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental procedures.

claim: The human FUS transgene was mostly confined to the CNS with little or no expression in other tissues.
source: The human FUS transgene (detected with an antibody to the HA-tag) was mostly confined to the CNS [with little or no expression in other tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)], in a pattern mimicking endogenous FUS in nuclei of NeuN-positive neurons (Figure 1B–C), GFAP-positive astrocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and CC1-positive oligodendrocytes of spinal cords (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) as well as in most regions of the brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Endogenous mouse FUS was reduced to 30-60% of non-transgenic level in all six established transgenic lines.
source: Endogenous mouse FUS was reduced both at the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B) and mRNA levels to 30–60% of non-transgenic level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and D) in all six established transgenic lines, consistent with an autoregulatory mechanism acting at the FUS RNA levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Spinal cord motor neurons expressing higher levels of human FUS had near complete elimination of mouse FUS.
source: Spinal cord motor neurons expressing higher levels of human FUS (cells labeled as 1, 2, 3, 4, five in Figure 1G) had near complete elimination of mouse FUS, while the subset of neurons without detectable human FUS retained a level of mouse FUS indistinguishable from that in mouse neurons of non-transgenic animals (cells labeled as 6, 7, eight in Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: All FUS transgenic animals developed age-dependent abnormal posture, abnormal clasping response, reduced hind limb spread, and progressively abnormal gait.
source: Although transgenic mice from all three genotypes appeared normal at birth and developed normal weight into adulthood, all FUS transgenic animals expressing wild type or ALS-linked mutations in which human FUS accumulated to at least half the FUS level in normal mice developed age-dependent abnormal posture, with lower stance and hunched back, an abnormal clasping response, reduced hind limb spread (upper panel of Figure 2A), and a progressively abnormal gait (lower panel of Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Shorter front and hind-limb stride-length developed by 12 months of age in all FUS transgenic lines.
source: While all genotypes displayed normal stride-length at two-months of age, shorter front and hind-limb stride-length developed by 12 months of age (Figure 2B) in all FUS transgenic lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by gait analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: High-frequency spontaneous firings of motor units (fibrillations) were recorded in 12-month-old FUS transgenic mice.
source: Similar fibrillations, albeit less frequent, were observed in all 12-month-old FUS transgenic mice, which were absent in non-transgenic littermates (Figure 2C), indicating widespread denervation of neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) and motor unit degeneration and regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG recording data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Up to ~30% of neuromuscular junctions were lost by 12 months of age in FUS transgenic mice.
source: While muscles were fully innervated at 2 months of age in all FUS transgenic mice, up to ~30% of the NMJs were lost by 12 months of age (Figure 2D), consistent with the abnormalities detected by EMG.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Age-dependent loss of large caliber motor axons was observed in 12-month-old FUSWT and FUSR514G mice.
source: This was accompanied by an age-dependent loss of large (>8.5 μm) caliber motor axons in 12-month-old FUSWT and FUSR514G mice compared to non-transgenic littermates (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), although no significant loss of motor axons was observed in aged FUSR521C mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by toluidine blue staining and quantification shown in Figure 2E and supplementary figures.

claim: Sensory axons of the L5 root were lost in an age-dependent manner in all three transgenic FUS lines (18-26% reduction by 12 months of age).
source: Sensory axons of the L5 root were lost in an age-dependent manner in all three transgenic FUS lines (18 ~ 26% reduction by 12 months of age) compared to non-transgenic controls (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F and supplementary figures.

claim: Age-dependent loss of motor neurons and increased astrogliosis were observed in 12-month-old transgenic FUS mice.
source: Finally, immunofluorescence analysis of the mouse lumbar spinal cords revealed age-dependent loss of motor neurons (Figure 2G; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) and increased astrogliosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) in 12-month-old transgenic FUSR514G, FUSR521C and FUSWT mice, compared to non-transgenic littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2G and supplementary figures.

claim: No homozygous animals were obtained for FUSR521C, suggesting that ALS-linked mutation in FUS may be more toxic than wild type FUS.
source: No homozygous animals were obtained for FUSR521C (despite production of multiple litters), suggesting that ALS-linked mutation in FUS may be more toxic than the wild type FUS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that no homozygous FUSR521C animals were obtained.

claim: A dose-dependent down-regulation of endogenous FUS and increased accumulation of total FUS exceeding twice the normal level was achieved in doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT animals.
source: As predicted, a dose-dependent down-regulation of endogenous FUS and increased accumulation of total FUS exceeding twice the protein level that found in non-transgenic spinal cord homogenates was achieved in the viable doubly hemizygous (line 101 crossed with line 136), and homozygous (line 101) FUSWT animals compared to singly hemizygous (line 101 and 136) FUSWT transgenic littermates (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice rapidly developed neurological disease as early as 2 weeks of age.
source: While the doubly hemizygous (line 101 crossed with line 136), and homozygous (line 101) FUSWT transgenic mice appeared normal at birth, they rapidly developed neurological disease as early as 2 weeks of age, including abnormal clasping (upper panel of Figure 3C) and abnormal gait (lower panel of Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: None of the doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice survived beyond 40 days of age.
source: These doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice eventually developed paralysis. None survived beyond 40 days of age (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice developed drastic (~92%) denervation of neuromuscular junctions by 30 days of age.
source: Doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice developed by 30 day of age drastic (~92%) denervation of neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) of the gastrocnemius muscle when compared with the age-matched non-transgenic littermates and singly hemizygous FUSWT mice (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Significant degeneration and loss of motor axons (29% and 35% in doubly hemizygotes, 19% and 23% in homozygotes) and spinal cord motor neurons were observed in 30-day-old FUS overexpressing mice.
source: This severe denervation was accompanied by significant degeneration and loss of motor axons (Figure 4C–D) and spinal cord motor neurons in 30-day-old doubly hemizygotes (29% and 35%, respectively) and homozygotes of FUSWT mice (19% and 23%, respectively) compared to non-transgenic littermates or singly hemizygous FUSWT mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by toluidine blue staining and quantification data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Sensory axons of the L5 root were lost (~30% reduction) in doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice.
source: Sensory axons of the L5 root were also lost (~30% reduction) in doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant increase in microgliosis and astrogliosis was observed in the lumbar spinal cords of doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice.
source: Despite near absence of both endogenous mouse and human FUS accumulation in microglia (<5% of cells are co-labeled with Iba-1 staining) (Figure 5D), a significant increase in microgliosis and astrogliosis (scored with Iba-I and GFAP immunoreactivity, respectively) in the lumbar spinal cords of doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) was observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: RNAs in non-transgenic and hemizygous FUSWT mice were almost indistinguishable at 30 days of age (only 7 RNA changes).
source: Although RNAs in non-transgenic and hemizygous FUSWT mice were almost indistinguishable at this age (only 7 RNA changes in comparing heterozygous FUSWT and non-transgenic mice) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), principal component analysis (PCA) and unsupervised hierarchical clustering revealed that homozygous FUSWT animals had a highly distinct RNA profile (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and PCA analysis shown in Figure 6A-B and supplementary figures.

claim: Comparison of RNAs from 30 day-old non-transgenic and homozygous FUSWT mice revealed 4081 expression changes (2228 up-regulated and 1853 down-regulated genes).
source: Comparison of RNAs from 30 day-old non-transgenic and homozygous FUSWT mice revealed 4081 expression changes (FDR corrected p<0.1, effect size > √2), with 2228 up- and 1853 down-regulated genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 15.1% of up-regulated genes and 26.1% of down-regulated genes are bound by FUS.
source: Based on the known FUS-binding sites (Lagier-Tourenne et al., 2012), 15.1% of up-regulated genes (337 out of 2228 genes) and 26.1% of down-regulated genes (483 out of 1853 genes) are bound by FUS.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with known FUS-binding sites from a cited study.

claim: The top up-regulated GO categories are involved in defense response, innate immune response and regulation of immune system process.
source: The top up-regulated GO categories are involved in defense response, innate immune response and regulation of immune system process, whereas top down-regulated GO categories are primarily metabolic, including steroid biosynthesis, cellular nitrogen compound metabolism process and cholesterol biosynthesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1a-1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Accumulation of RNAs from genes with exceptionally long introns was reduced in both doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice.
source: Accumulation of the RNAs from these very long genes (including Kcnip4, Nkain2, Park2, Nrxn3, Pcdh9, Grm and Hs2st3) was also reduced in both doubly hemizygous (line 101 and line 136) and homozygous (line 101) FUSWT mice (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: All four genes encoding subunits of neuronal intermediate filaments and the motor neuron-specific gene Chat were down-regulated in spinal cords of doubly hemizygous and homozygous FUSWT mice.
source: Additionally, all four genes encoding subunits of neuronal intermediate filaments (Nefl, Nefm, Nefh, and Prph), together with the motor neuron-specific gene Chat, were down-regulated in spinal cords of doubly hemizygous and homozygous (line 101) FUSWT mice, compared to age-matched non-transgenic and either hemizygous mouse lines (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The majority of mRNAs showed comparable expression levels with those of control mice at P14, when the mice overexpressing FUS showed no apparent phenotype.
source: Of note, the majority of mRNAs showed comparable expression levels with those of control mice, when qRT-PCR were performed for the P14 mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 3). At this age, the mice overexpressing FUS showed no apparent phenotype (Figure 3), suggesting that the massive transcription changes at late stage are dominated by the effects of neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Genes passing the significance cutoff (FDR < 0.1) demonstrated a marked opposite-dominant pattern, with a conversely perturbed proportion of 0.629 ± 0.017.
source: Genes passing our significance cutoff (FDR < 0.1) demonstrated a marked opposite-dominant pattern, with a conversely perturbed proportion of 0.629 ± 0.017 (95% confidence interval) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by proportional analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The lower motor neuron disease associated with dose-dependent increased accumulation of human FUSWT is primarily driven by gain-of-toxicity rather than loss of function of endogenous FUS.
source: Taken together, the lower motor neuron disease associated with dose-dependent increased accumulation of human FUSWT, is primarily driven by gain-of-toxicity rather than loss of function of endogenous FUS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proportional analysis comparing FUS overexpression and knockdown.

claim: CNS-expression of wild type human FUS rescues the FUS-null lethality in mice.
source: While endogenous FUS-null mice in this background die shortly after birth, the FUSWT transgene complemented the essential FUS functions throughout early development albeit with lower Mendelian ratio (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by breeding data and immunoblot shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: Most RNA expression changes in FUSWT transgenic mice with both endogenous mouse alleles disrupted were nearly fully restored to their levels in non-transgenic mice.
source: Most were nearly fully restored to their levels in non-transgenic mice, confirming the functional rescue of FUS function, albeit the most-down regulated genes were only partially rescued (Figure 8C), suggesting that maturation of these RNAs is very sensitive to FUS level.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Wild type human FUS protein complements the loss of the endogenous mouse FUS protein.
source: Altogether the near complete rescue of RNA expression changes in the FUSWT transgenic mice with both endogenous mouse alleles disrupted indicates that wild type human FUS protein complements the loss of the endogenous mouse FUS protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Accumulation of p62/SQSTM1 was found in the motor neurons of homozygotes FUSWT mice, but not in non-transgenic and hemizygote FUSWT mice.
source: Although ubiquitin-positive aggregates were not observed (data not shown), accumulation of p62/SQSTM1 (sequestosome 1) accumulated found in the motor neurons of homozygotes FUSWT mice, but not the non-transgenic and hemizygote FUSWT mice nor neighboring non-motor neurons (Figure 9A), suggesting a potential autophagic deficit in these motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Increased expression of BFP-tagged wild-type FUS, FUSR514C, or FUSR521C almost completely inhibited nutrient deprivation driven autophagic activation.
source: However, increased expression of BFP-tagged wild-type FUS, FUSR514C, or FUSR521C almost completely inhibited nutrient deprivation driven autophagic activation (Figure 9E–F), with a significant reduction in the fraction of red puncta that correspond to autolysosomes and an increase in the number of autophagosomes (yellow puncta) (Figure 9C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by autophagy assay data shown in Figure 9C, E-F.

claim: Increased levels of FUSWT did not suppress the NLM-mediated p62 puncta accumulation, but rather increased the percentage of cells with p62 puncta.
source: However, increased levels of FUSWT did not suppress the NLM-mediated p62 puncta accumulation, but rather increased the percentage of cells with p62 puncta (Figure 9C,F), indicative of the compromised autophagic flux pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9C, F.

claim: Increased expression of wild-type or ALS-linked FUS mutants inhibits autophagy.
source: These findings indicate that increased expression of wild-type or either of these ALS-linked FUS mutants inhibits autophagy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the autophagy assay data shown in Figure 9.

claim: FUS autoregulates its own protein expression level in the CNS.
source: Furthermore, FUS autoregulates its own protein expression level in the CNS.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: An increase in expression of wild type FUS can saturate the autoregulatory mechanism and sharply accelerate disease phenotypes and trigger early mortality.
source: An increase in expression of wild type FUS can saturate this autoregulation and thereby sharply accelerates disease phenotypes and triggers early mortality accompanied by disturbances in both protein homeostasis and RNA processing (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings shown in Figure 3 and subsequent analyses.

claim: Disruption of FUS homeostasis incurs gain-of-function toxicity directed against autophagy and loss-of RNA processing function.
source: Thus, disruption of FUS homeostasis incurs gain-of-function toxicity directed against autophagy and loss-of RNA processing function, thereby providing an explanation for how FUS can promote disease pathogenesis in the absence of mutation (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: FUS auto-regulation is known to maintain normal FUS levels and the underlying mechanisms have been previously described in cultured cells and in a humanized FUS mouse model.
source: FUS auto-regulation is known to maintain normal FUS levels and the underlying mechanisms have been previously described in cultured cells (Zhou et al., 2013; Dini Modigliani et al., 2014) and in a recent humanized FUS mouse model (López-Erauskin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FUSWT mice are less affected compared with FUSR514G mice, suggesting a mutant-enhanced toxicity.
source: In addition, FUSWT mice are less affected compared with FUSR514G mice, suggesting a mutant-enhanced toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of phenotypes between different transgenic lines.

claim: Expression of R521C in mice did not produce motor axon loss, but rather sensory axon loss, which differs from FUS-related ALS in humans.
source: Furthermore, although R521C mutation is one of the most frequent FUS mutations in ALS, expression of R521C in mice did not produce motor axon loss, but rather sensory axon loss, which differs from the FUS-related ALS in human.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Wild-type and R514G transgenes produce both motor and sensory axon degeneration.
source: By contrast, wild-type and R514G transgene produce both the motor and sensory axon degeneration.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The homeostatic levels of FUS are essential for proper neuron function, as a 2-fold increase in FUS levels accelerated the disease at least 5-fold.
source: More importantly, we uncovered that the homeostatic levels of FUS are essential for proper neuron function, as a 2-fold increase in FUS levels accelerated the disease at least 5-fold (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of disease progression in different transgenic lines.

claim: Elevated expression levels of genes encoding pathological hallmarks are not without precedent in other neurodegenerative diseases, such as duplication of the APP gene and locus triplication of α-synuclein.
source: Elevated expression levels of genes encoding the pathological hallmarks are not without precedent in other neurodegenerative diseases, such as duplication of the APP gene (amyloid precursor protein, causal for Alzheimer's disease) (Sleegers et al., 2006), and locus triplication of α-synuclein (causal for Parkinson's disease) (Singleton et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on other neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Variants within the 3'-UTR of TARDBP gene can lead to increased TDP-43 expression and have been reported for FTD.
source: Similar findings, that variants within the 3'-UTR of TARDBP gene can lead to increased TDP-43 expression, have also been reported for FTD (Gitcho et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gitcho et al., 2009.

claim: Genome-wide expression profiling reveals gene changes that are largely distinct with FUS-knockdown using antisense oligonucleotides.
source: Furthermore, genome-wide expression profiling reveals gene changes that are largely distinct with FUS-knockdown using antisense oligonucleotides.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the comparative transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: It is unlikely that FUS-mediated ALS is initiated by the loss-of-FUS-function.
source: Indeed, work by Kino and colleagues showed that the behavior and pathological phenotypes caused by FUS deletion are largely distinct from those observed in ALS (Kino et al., 2015), thereby supporting the notion that it is unlikely that FUS-mediated ALS is initiated by the loss-of-FUS-function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison with cited work by Kino et al., 2015.

claim: Similar biological processes, such as synaptic functions, myelination, and immune response, can be affected by either increased or lowered levels of FUS.
source: For example, similar biological processes, such as synaptic functions, myelination, and immune response, can be affected by either increased or lowered levels of FUS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: FUS-OE and FUS-KD may have opposite effects on mitochondrial function.
source: Conversely, FUS-OE and FUS-KD may have opposite effects on mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: A likely scenario is that the toxic cascade is initiated at the nucleus with dysregulation of RNA processing being one of the potential mechanisms, and subsequently, is exacerbated by the loss of nuclear FUS.
source: As (i) FUS pathology is associated with loss of nuclear FUS and concomitant cytosolic FUS accumulation (Neumann et al., 2009; Dormann et al., 2010), and (ii) the strong phenotype produced by over-expression of wild type FUS did not correlate with FUS aggregation as the majority of FUS remains in the nucleus, a likely scenario is that the toxic cascade is initiated at the nucleus with dysregulation of RNA processing being one of the potential mechanisms, and subsequently, is exacerbated by the loss of nuclear FUS.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: Increased FUS expression (wild type or disease-linked mutants) is sufficient to inhibit autophagy induction and flux using both LC3 and p62 as markers.
source: We showed here that increased FUS expression (wild type or disease-linked mutants) is sufficient to inhibit autophagy induction and flux using both LC3 and p62 as markers (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by autophagy assay data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The majority of FUS protein remained in the nucleus of motor neurons, but not in other cells, in the spinal cord and co-localized with p62.
source: Interestingly, the majority of FUS protein remained in the nucleus of motor neurons, but not in other cells, in the spinal cord and co-localized with p62 (Figure 9), suggesting perturbed protein homeostasis in motor neurons and that motor neurons may be more susceptible to elevated FUS levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Reactive astrocytes become apparent in lumbar spinal cord sections of all three genotypes in aged (10-12 month-old) animals.
source: Activation of astrocytes (astrogliosis) is one hallmark of ALS pathology (Schiffer et al., 1996). Reactive astrocytes become apparent in lumbar spinal cord sections of in all three genotypes in aged (10 ~ 12 month-old) animals.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, with a citation to Schiffer et al., 1996 for background.

claim: Neither endogenous nor transgenic FUS is expressed in microglia.
source: However, in contrast to SOD1-mediated toxicity, it appears that neither endogenous nor transgenic FUS is expressed in microglia (Figure 5, see also (Qiu et al., 2014)), suggesting that disease pathogenesis is not driven by FUS-mediated toxicity within the microglia.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5 and a citation to Qiu et al., 2014.

claim: The FUS mouse models developed age-dependent and mutant-enhanced phenotypes.
source: In conclusion, our FUS mouse models resemble the endogenous FUS expression pattern and levels and developed age-dependent and mutant-enhanced phenotypes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the overall findings from the study.

claim: Elevated FUS levels produce gain-of-toxic properties by overriding FUS autoregulation, disrupting protein and RNA homeostasis.
source: We provide evidence that elevated FUS levels produce gain-of-toxic properties by overriding FUS autoregulation, disrupting protein and RNA homeostasis.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the overall findings from the study.

claim: These disruptions are, at least in part, due to autophagy inhibition causing proteotoxic stress and a loss of normal RNA processing function.
source: These disruptions are, at least in part, due to autophagy inhibition causing proteotoxic stress and a loss of normal RNA processing function, in which genes with long transcripts and involved in synaptic function are selectively affected.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the overall findings from the study.

claim: Maintaining FUS homeostasis, which in turn is required for proper protein and RNA homeostasis, is essential for normal neuron function.
source: Thus, maintaining FUS homeostasis, which in turn is required for proper protein and RNA homeostasis, is essential for normal neuron function (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: The three FUS transgenes (FUSWT, FUSR514G and FUSR521C) accumulated to 0.5 to 1.5-fold the level of mouse FUS.
source: The three FUS transgenes (FUSWT, FUSR514G and FUSR521C) accumulated to 0.5 to 1.5-fold the level of mouse FUS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B) (as determined by immunoblotting brain extracts using an antibody that recognizes human and mouse FUS protein with comparable affinity [López-Erauskin et al., 2018]).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: An auto-regulatory mechanism regulates FUS mRNA stability or maturation to maintain FUS level within individual cells of the mouse central nervous system (CNS).
source: Collectively, we conclude that an auto-regulatory mechanism regulating FUS mRNA stability or maturation to maintain FUS level within individual cells of the mouse central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of human FUS at levels between 0.7 and 1.2 of the normal mouse FUS level produces age-dependent, selective denervation and degeneration of lower motor axons.
source: Taken together, expression of human FUS at levels between 0.7 and 1.2 of the normal mouse FUS level produces age-dependent, selective denervation and degeneration of lower motor axons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Increased accumulation of FUS to 2-fold above its normal level is sufficient to produce age-dependent, fatal motor neuron disease.
source: Altogether, increased accumulation of FUS to 2-fold above its normal level is sufficient to produce age-dependent, fatal motor neuron disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Increasing FUS levels by as little as 2-fold produces a counterintuitive, apparent loss of FUS function for maturation of the pre-mRNAs encoded by genes with exceptionally long introns.
source: Taken together, the data suggest that neurons are more susceptible to the increasing wild type human FUS levels, and increasing FUS levels by as little as 2-fold produces a counterintuitive, apparent loss of FUS function for maturation of the pre-mRNAs encoded by genes with exceptionally long introns.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: FUS over-expression does not induce widespread transcription changes at P14, but does lead to toxicity, and at late stages, this involves alterations in RNA metabolism and autophagy.
source: Therefore, FUS over-expression does not induce widespread transcription changes at P14, but does lead to toxicity, and at late stages, this involves alterations in RNA metabolism (Figure 6E) and autophagy (see below).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of transcriptome data at different time points.

claim: 23% of oppositely-regulated mRNAs and 31% of co-regulated mRNAs are bound by FUS.
source: Based on the known FUS-binding sites (Lagier-Tourenne et al., 2012), 23% of oppositely-regulated mRNAs (conversely perturbed category: expression changes are in opposing directions in FUS over-expression and knockdown conditions, 199 out of 862 genes) and 31% of co-regulated mRNAs (similarly perturbed category: the directions of expression change are the same in both FUS over-expression and knockdown conditions, 158 out of 507 genes) are bound by FUS.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with known FUS-binding sites from a cited study.

claim: FUS-OE and FUS-KD can have opposite effects on mitochondrial functions.
source: These findings suggest that (1) similar biological process, such as synaptic functions and immune response, can be affected in the similar fashion by FUS-OE and FUS-KD, and conversely, (2) FUS-OE and FUS-KD can have opposite effects on other biological pathways, such as mitochondrial functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Wild type human FUS protein complements the loss of the endogenous mouse FUS protein, confirming the functional rescue of FUS function.
source: Most were nearly fully restored to their levels in non-transgenic mice, confirming the functional rescue of FUS function, albeit the most-down regulated genes were only partially rescued (Figure 8C), suggesting that maturation of these RNAs is very sensitive to FUS level.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Even a slight imbalance of FUS level is critical for its proper function in the CNS and increasing FUS level exerts gain-of-toxic effects.
source: Taken together, these genetic and genomic data suggest that even a slight imbalance of FUS level is critical for its proper function in the CNS and increasing FUS level exerts gain-of-toxic effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiment and comparative transcriptome analysis.

claim: Upregulation of lysosomal genes in the homozygous FUSWT mice suggests changes in the status of protein homeostasis.
source: Upregulation of lysosomal genes in the homozygous FUSWT mice suggests changes in the status of protein homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing upregulation of lysosomal genes.

claim: The majority of FUS was nuclear, with only a small portion in the cytosol in the neurons of homozygous FUSWT mice.
source: The majority of FUS was nuclear, with only a small portion in the cytosol in the neurons of homozygous FUSWT mice (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Ubiquitin-positive aggregates were not observed in homozygous FUSWT mice.
source: Although ubiquitin-positive aggregates were not observed (data not shown), accumulation of p62/SQSTM1 (sequestosome 1) accumulated found in the motor neurons of homozygotes FUSWT mice, but not the non-transgenic and hemizygote FUSWT mice nor neighboring non-motor neurons (Figure 9A), suggesting a potential autophagic deficit in these motor neurons.
evidence: This is a negative observation from the experimental data.

claim: Robust autophagy was induced in 45% of Neuro2A cells transiently expressing mCherry-GFP-LC3 and BFP after 8 hr of NLM treatment.
source: As expected, after 8 hr of NLM treatment of Neuro2A cells transiently expressing mCherry-GFP-LC3 and the blue fluorescence protein (BFP) as a control, robust autophagy (setting >7 puncta for autophagy activation) was induced as revealed by the accumulation of LC3 puncta in 45% of the cells (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by autophagy assay data shown in Figure 9C-D.

claim: p62 puncta accumulation was reduced in Neuro2A cells expressing BFP upon NLM addition.
source: As anticipated, p62 puncta accumulation was reduced in Neuro2A cells expressing BFP upon NLM addition (Figure 9C, two right top and middle panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Human FUS and its ALS-linked mutations (R514G and R521C) were fused to an N-terminal hemagglutinin (HA) tag and placed under the control of the murine prion promoter.
source: cDNAs for human wild type (hereafter referred as FUSWT) and either of two ALS-linked mutants of FUS, R514G (arginine to glycine substitution at amino acid 514, hereafter referred as FUSR514G) and R521C (arginine to cysteine substitution at amino acid 521, hereafter referred as FUSR521C) were fused to a N-terminal hemagglutinin (HA) tag and placed under the control of the murine prion promoter (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Each transgene was flanked with loxP sites to permit deletion in the presence of Cre recombinase activity.
source: Each transgene was flanked with loxP sites to permit deletion in the presence of Cre recombinase activity.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The human FUS transgene was expressed in neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes of spinal cords as well as in most regions of the brain.
source: The human FUS transgene (detected with an antibody to the HA-tag) was mostly confined to the CNS [with little or no expression in other tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)], in a pattern mimicking endogenous FUS in nuclei of NeuN-positive neurons (Figure 1B–C), GFAP-positive astrocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), and CC1-positive oligodendrocytes of spinal cords (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) as well as in most regions of the brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Lines with most comparable levels of wild type and mutant human and mouse FUS proteins were selected for further characterization.
source: Lines with most comparable levels of wild type (line 101 for FUSWT) and mutant (line 124 for FUSR514G and line 135 for FUSR521C) human and mouse FUS proteins (Figure 1D,E) were selected for further characterization.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.
